name: Amnon
title: David's firstborn son
summary: Amnon was the eldest of King David's sons and was born in Hebron. His mother was Ahinoam from Jezreel. As the firstborn, he initially held a prominent position in the line of succession, but his actions led to his own downfall. He violated his half-sister Tamar through a cunning plan devised together with his cousin Jonadab. The assault triggered a chain of violence and grief within David's royal family: Absalom harbored silent hatred for two years before he had his servants kill Amnon during a sheep-shearing feast at Baal-Hazor. This entire tragic sequence of events reflects the judgment that the prophet Nathan pronounced over David's house after the king's own sin with Bathsheba, and shows how violence and injustice are passed from generation to generation when justice is absent.

keyEvents.title: Born as David's firstborn in Hebron
keyEvents.description: Amnon was born in Hebron as David's firstborn son during his reign over Judah. His mother was Ahinoam from Jezreel.

keyEvents.title: Lust for Half-Sister Tamar
keyEvents.description: Amnon was seized by an intense lust for his beautiful half-sister Tamar, Absalom's sister. The desire tormented him so severely that he fell ill, since she was a virgin and it seemed impossible for him to approach her.

keyEvents.title: Jonadab's Devious Plan
keyEvents.description: Amnon's cousin Jonadab, described as a cunning man, advised him to pretend to be sick and ask King David to send Tamar to prepare food at his bedside—so that he could have her alone.

keyEvents.title: The Assault on Tamar
keyEvents.description: Amnon brought Tamar into his bedroom and raped her despite her earnest pleas and protests. Immediately afterward, the lust turned into intense hatred, and he drove her away in disgrace.

keyEvents.title: David's Anger and Passivity
keyEvents.description: When King David learned what had happened, he was greatly angered, but he did not intervene to punish Amnon. This passivity contributed to Absalom taking revenge into his own hands.

keyEvents.title: Absalom's Revenge and Amnon's Death
keyEvents.description: Two years after the assault, Absalom invited all the king's sons to a sheep-shearing festival in Baal-Hazor. When Amnon had become drunk, Absalom ordered his servants to kill him—a long-planned act of revenge for what he had done to Tamar.

versions.reason: [critical] The role is set to 'princess' (feminine), but Amnon was a male person. The correct role should be 'prince' or an equivalent masculine form.; [minor] The summary is good, but could include a brief theological reflection on how Amnon's actions are part of Nathan's prophecy that "the sword shall never depart from your house" (2 Sam 12:10) as a consequence of David's sin.; [minor] In the event "Desire for Tamar," the expression "sick with love" is used – this should be nuanced, as it was desire/lust, not love in the biblical sense. The text may give a misleading impression.; [major] There are no footnotes that can shed light on historical, linguistic, or theological aspects of this important story.; [minor] The list of siblings is reasonable, but it should be noted that Tamar is listed as a sibling – she was technically a half-sister (daughter of David and Maaka). It is correct to include her, but the distinctions are worth noting.; [minor] Lifespan "c. 1000 BC" is very approximate. Amnon was born in Hebron during David's reign over Judah (c. 1010–1003 BC) and killed about two years after the rape of Tamar. A more precise indication could be "c. 1010–990 BC," although exact dates are uncertain.

versions.summary: Amnon was King David's firstborn son, born to Ahinoam of Jezreel while David reigned in Hebron. He is best known for his shameful rape of his half-sister Tamar, an act that had serious consequences within David's family. Two years later, Amnon was killed by his half-brother Absalom as revenge for the crime. This tragic sequence of events was part of the fulfillment of the prophet Nathan's words of judgment against David's house after the sin with Bathsheba, and illustrates how sin breeds destruction within a family.

footnotes.text: The name Amnon (אַמְנוֹן) is derived from the Hebrew root 'aman' (אמן), meaning 'faithful' or 'reliable'. This stands in stark ironic contrast to his actions, which were marked by betrayal and unfaithfulness toward his own sister and family.

Jonadab is described with the Hebrew word חָכָם (chakam), usually translated as 'wise' or 'prudent'. The word is most often used positively in the Hebrew Bible, but here it demonstrates how intellectual sharpness can be turned to evil—a thematic parallel to the serpent's cunning (עָרוּם) in Gen 3:1.

Amnon's abuse and Absalom's bloody revenge form a central part of the fulfillment of the prophet Nathan's word of judgment: 'The sword shall never depart from your house' (2 Sam 12:10). The story serves as a narrative example of how unresolved sin spreads like ripples in water within a dynastic family.

Sheep shearing (גֵּז) was one of the most important economic events in ancient Israel's agricultural society. It was often marked by feasts and banquets, which gave Absalom a natural opportunity to gather the king's sons without arousing suspicion.

In rabbinic tradition (Sanhedrin 21a), the question is discussed whether Tamar was Amnon's half-sister in a halachic sense. Some rabbis claimed that Tamar's mother Maaka became pregnant before she converted to Judaism, which would have made Tamar halachically unrelated to Amnon – and thus a lawful marriage would have been possible, as Tamar herself suggested (2 Sam 13:13).

David's reaction to the rape is described as him becoming 'very angry' (2 Sam 13:21), but he apparently did nothing. The Greek translation Septuaginta adds that David would not harm his firstborn son Amnon because he loved him. This passivity on David's part contributed to Absalom taking matters into his own hands, which further escalated the conflict.
